hints: Look at the functional group in each structure first. Which of P, Q and R contains an $\text{O-H}$ group, and which contain a $\text{C=O}$ group?

Recall what each test reagent detects. Think about which type of compound gives effervescence with $\text{Na}$, which gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, and which can be oxidised by acidified dichromate.
Remember the difference between aldehydes and ketones toward oxidation. Only one of Q and R can turn orange dichromate green.
walkthrough:
Sort out what P, Q and R actually are**
Look closely. P has an $\text{-OH}$ on a carbon with no H attached plus a $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group, so it is a tertiary alcohol and a nitrile. It has no $\text{C=O}$. Q is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, a ketone. R is $\text{OHC-CH=CH-CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, an aldehyde with a $\text{C=C}$ bond.

Decide the sodium results**
Sodium reacts with the acidic H in $\text{O-H}$ groups to give $\text{H}_2$ gas seen as effervescence. Only P has an alcohol $\text{O-H}$. Q and R have no $\text{O-H}$, so P gives effervescence, Q and R show no reaction.

Decide the 2,4-DNPH results**
2,4-DNPH gives an orange precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone because of addition to the $\text{C=O}$ bond. Q is a ketone and R is an aldehyde, so both give an orange precipitate. P has no $\text{C=O}$, so no reaction, as already given.

Decide the acidified dichromate results**
Acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ is an oxidising agent that turns from orange to green when it oxidises a primary or secondary alcohol or an aldehyde. R is an aldehyde so it is oxidised and the solution turns green. Q is a ketone and is not oxidised. P is a tertiary alcohol and is not oxidised, so both show no reaction.

Final answer: Na(s): P effervescence, Q no reaction, R no reaction
2,4-DNPH: P no reaction, Q orange ppt, R orange ppt
acidified $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7(aq)}$: P no reaction, Q no reaction, R turns green

hints: Think about what reduction does to a ketone $\text{C=O}$. How many $\text{[H]}$ atoms are needed to convert $\text{C=O}$ into $\text{CH-OH}$?
walkthrough:
See reduction as adding hydrogen across C=O**
Q is the ketone $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. $\text{NaBH}_4$ acts as a source of hydrogen, written as $\text{[H]}$. The $\text{C=O}$ gains two H atoms, one on C and one on O, to become a secondary alcohol $\text{CH-OH}$. So you need $2\text{[H]}$: $$\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O} + 2\text{[H]} \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$$

hints: Look at the $\text{C=C}$ bond in R. Check whether each C of the double bond carries two different groups.
Compare the positions of the two H atoms in the drawn R. Think about what arrangement would place the large groups on the same side instead of opposite sides.
walkthrough:
Spot why geometric isomerism is possible**
R contains $\text{C=C}$. Rotation about the double bond is restricted because the pi bond would have to break. On the left C the two groups are $\text{OHC}$ and $\text{H}$, which are different. On the right C the two groups are $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which are different. So cis-trans or geometric isomerism occurs.

Draw the opposite arrangement**
The structure shown has $\text{OHC}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ on opposite sides, a trans arrangement. The other stereoisomer simply swaps them to the same side. Draw $\text{C=C}$ horizontally, put $\text{OHC}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ both above the bond and both H atoms both below the bond: $$\text{OHC-C(H)=C(H)-CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \text{ (cis)}$$ Keep the connectivity identical, only the spatial positions change.

Final answer: type of stereoisomerism: geometric(al) (cis-trans)
other stereoisomer: $\mathrm{OHC-C(H)=C(H)-CH_2CH_3}$ with $\mathrm{OHC}$ and $\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}$ on the same side of $\mathrm{C=C}$ (cis isomer, both H atoms on the other side)

hints: Scan the spectrum only above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Note the positions of the two strong broad or sharp dips, one near $3400 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and one near $2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.

Recall the characteristic IR regions: $\text{O-H}$ gives a broad absorption around $3200$-$3600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ absorbs near $2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$, while aldehyde and ketone $\text{C=O}$ absorbs near $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
Match those two key absorptions to the functional groups present in only one of P, Q or R.
walkthrough:
Read the two diagnostic peaks**
Focus above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ as instructed. There is a broad strong absorption centred near $3400 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ in the $3100$-$3700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ region, and a sharp absorption at about $2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. There is no strong peak at about $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ where $\text{C=O}$ would appear.

Assign bonds to the peaks**
The broad peak at $3100$-$3700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the $\text{O-H}$ stretch, broadened by hydrogen bonding. The sharp peak at $2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ stretch. Both are characteristic and listed in the Data Booklet.

Link to P, Q or R**
Only P has both an alcohol $\text{O-H}$ and a nitrile $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. Q is a ketone and R is an aldehyde, both would show a strong $\text{C=O}$ stretch near $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and neither contains $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. So the spectrum must be P.

Final answer: compound P
explanation: absorption at $2250 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ stretch AND absorption at $3100$-$3700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{O-H}$ stretch. Only P contains both $\text{O-H}$ and $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$; Q and R contain $\text{C=O}$ which would absorb near $1700 \text{ cm}^{-1}$.
